title: GOVT. T. ROMANA COLLEGE NOTES
VALUE ADDED COURSE (VAC)
BATCH 4 — VAC 104
HEALTH AND WELLNESS
WHOLE SYLLABUS • SHORT NOTES & LONG NOTES
2 Credits | For use by students of Govt. T. Romana College only.
blocks: If you are not taking VAC 104 – Health and Wellness, there is no need to study this section.
This is a universal Value Added Course. Medical and scientific terms are explained in simple college-level English so that students from any subject can follow them.

The official syllabus has two units of 15 lectures each. Unit I introduces health, wellness, nutrition, common diseases and mental health. Unit II deals with the management of health and wellness through fitness, exercise, posture, meditation, sleep and the prevention of substance abuse.

For short answers, learn the definition, the main types or causes, and two or three points on prevention or management. For long answers, explain the concept, give examples and end with practical measures.
These notes are for learning and examination preparation. They are not a substitute for medical advice; anyone with a health problem should consult a qualified doctor or counsellor.

According to the syllabus, the course aims to help students understand the importance of a healthy lifestyle, to give a general understanding of physical and mental health, to create awareness of lifestyle-related diseases and to provide an understanding of stress management. The programme outcomes are that students maintain healthy lifestyles, learn how to cope with challenges in life and are able to demonstrate life skills.
UNIT I — INTRODUCTION TO HEALTH & WELLNESS

The World Health Organization (WHO), in its Constitution (1948), defines health as 'a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity'. This definition shows that health has several dimensions and is not only about the body.

Health is often described as having physical, mental, social and spiritual dimensions. A person may be free of disease but still not fully healthy if they are under constant stress or socially isolated.
Wellness is an active, lifelong process of making choices that lead to a healthy and fulfilling life. The American physician Halbert L. Dunn popularized the idea of 'high-level wellness' in 1961.
Wellness is commonly described in dimensions: physical, emotional, intellectual, social, spiritual, occupational, environmental and financial wellness. Each dimension affects the others.

Health is a state of being, while wellness is a process of actively working towards a better state. Health can be affected by factors beyond our control, such as genes or an accident, while wellness focuses on the choices we can make, such as diet, exercise, sleep and relationships.

A person with a chronic illness, such as diabetes, can still practise wellness by managing the condition well, staying active and keeping a positive outlook. Health is the goal; wellness is the way of living that supports it.

The main factors are heredity (genes), lifestyle (diet, physical activity, sleep, tobacco and alcohol use), the physical environment (clean water, air, sanitation, housing), the social and economic environment (income, education, employment, family and community support), and access to health services.

Culture, gender, age and personal behaviour also matter. The WHO calls these the 'determinants of health'. Many of them, such as diet and activity, can be changed by individuals, while others need action by families, communities and governments.

Malnutrition means an imbalance in a person's intake of energy and nutrients. The WHO uses the term to cover both undernutrition and overnutrition, so a person can be malnourished by eating too little or too much of the wrong foods.

Malnutrition affects growth, immunity, learning, work capacity and the risk of disease. In India, the POSHAN Abhiyaan (National Nutrition Mission), launched in 2018, aims to reduce stunting, undernutrition, anaemia and low birth weight.

Undernutrition results from not eating enough food or enough nutrients. It includes stunting (low height for age), wasting (low weight for height), underweight (low weight for age) and micronutrient deficiencies such as iron-deficiency anaemia, vitamin A deficiency and iodine deficiency.

According to the National Family Health Survey-5 (2019-21), about 35.5 per cent of Indian children under five were stunted and about 57 per cent of women aged 15-49 were anaemic. Undernutrition weakens immunity and can harm brain development in children.

Overnutrition is the excessive intake of energy, often from foods high in sugar, fat and salt, leading to overweight and obesity. It increases the risk of type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, some cancers and joint problems.

Body Mass Index (BMI) is weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in metres. By WHO adult standards, a BMI of 18.5-24.9 is normal, 25-29.9 is overweight and 30 or above is obese. Lower cut-offs are often recommended for Asian populations because health risks begin at a lower BMI.

The human body works through several systems: the digestive system (gastritis, peptic ulcer, diarrhoea), the respiratory system (asthma, tuberculosis, pneumonia), the circulatory system (hypertension, coronary heart disease, stroke), the nervous system (migraine, epilepsy), the skeletal and muscular systems (arthritis, osteoporosis, back pain), the excretory system (kidney stones, urinary tract infections), the endocrine system (diabetes, thyroid disorders) and the immune system (allergies, HIV/AIDS).

Diseases may be communicable (spread from person to person, such as tuberculosis, malaria and hepatitis) or non-communicable (not spread by contact, such as diabetes, heart disease and cancer). Non-communicable diseases are now the leading cause of death in India.
A sedentary lifestyle means spending most of the day sitting or lying down with very little physical activity, for example long hours at a desk, in front of screens or in vehicles.

Physical inactivity raises the risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, high blood pressure, some cancers, weak bones and depression. The WHO recommends that adults do at least 150-300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity (or 75-150 minutes of vigorous activity) every week, and that children and adolescents aged 5-17 average at least 60 minutes a day.

A healthy diet includes plenty of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, pulses, nuts and seeds, with moderate amounts of fish, eggs, lean meat and low-fat dairy. The WHO advises eating at least 400 g of fruit and vegetables a day, keeping salt below 5 g a day and keeping free sugars below 10 per cent of total energy.

For hypertension, a low-salt diet rich in fruits and vegetables (such as the DASH diet) helps. For diabetes, whole grains and other low glycaemic index foods, fibre and regular meal timing help control blood sugar. For heart disease, foods with healthy fats and fibre are recommended, while trans fats and excess saturated fat should be avoided. For cancer prevention, a diet rich in fibre, fruits and vegetables and low in processed meat, alcohol and very salty or smoked foods is advised. For obesity and Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS), a balanced, portion-controlled, low-glycaemic diet with regular exercise supports weight management and hormonal balance.

Stress is the body's and mind's response to demands or threats that a person sees as challenging. A little stress (eustress) can motivate us, but long-term or excessive stress (distress) harms health.

Hans Selye described the General Adaptation Syndrome, with three stages: alarm, resistance and exhaustion. Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman, in 'Stress, Appraisal and Coping' (1984), explained that stress depends on how a person appraises a situation and their ability to cope.

Anxiety is a feeling of worry, nervousness or fear about what might happen. It is a normal reaction to danger, but it becomes a disorder when it is excessive, lasts a long time and interferes with daily life.

Symptoms include restlessness, rapid heartbeat, sweating, difficulty concentrating, sleep problems and avoidance of situations. Anxiety disorders include generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, social anxiety and phobias.

Depression is a common mental disorder marked by persistent sadness, loss of interest or pleasure in activities, low energy, changes in sleep and appetite, feelings of worthlessness or guilt, poor concentration and, in severe cases, thoughts of death or suicide. Doctors usually consider a diagnosis when such symptoms last for at least two weeks.

Depression is treatable through counselling, psychotherapy, medication when prescribed, social support and lifestyle changes such as regular exercise and sleep. In India, the Tele-MANAS mental health helpline (14416), launched in 2022, provides free counselling.
Biological factors include genes, brain chemistry, physical illness and hormonal changes. Psychological factors include personality, coping skills, self-esteem and past trauma.

Social and environmental factors include family relationships, peer pressure, academic or work pressure, poverty, unemployment, discrimination, loneliness, violence, substance use, excessive social media use and stigma about seeking help. Supportive relationships, a sense of purpose, physical activity and access to care protect mental health.
Health and Wellness: Meaning, Difference and Factors

Health, according to the WHO (1948), is 'a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity'. Wellness is the active process of making choices that lead towards this state. Health is a condition; wellness is a way of living.

Wellness has several dimensions: physical (exercise, nutrition, sleep), emotional (managing feelings and stress), intellectual (learning and creativity), social (healthy relationships), spiritual (meaning and values), occupational (satisfaction in work or study), environmental (clean and safe surroundings) and financial (managing money). A weakness in one dimension can affect the others.

Health and wellness are influenced by heredity, lifestyle, environment, socio-economic conditions, education, culture and access to health services. Lifestyle factors, such as diet, physical activity, sleep, tobacco and alcohol use, are especially important because they can be changed.
In conclusion, students should see health and wellness as their own responsibility as well as that of society, and should build habits that support all the dimensions of wellness.
Malnutrition is an imbalance between the body's needs and the intake of energy and nutrients. It includes undernutrition and overnutrition.

Undernutrition includes stunting, wasting, underweight and micronutrient deficiencies. It is caused by poverty, lack of food, poor diet quality, frequent infections, poor sanitation and lack of awareness. Its effects include weak immunity, delayed growth, poor learning, anaemia and low work capacity. NFHS-5 (2019-21) found that about 35.5 per cent of children under five in India were stunted.

Overnutrition leads to overweight and obesity. It is caused by diets high in sugar, fat, salt and processed foods, combined with physical inactivity. It raises the risk of diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, some cancers and PCOS. Many Indian families now face a 'double burden', with undernutrition and obesity existing in the same community or even the same household.

Measures include a balanced diet, nutrition education, food fortification, programmes such as POSHAN Abhiyaan, the mid-day meal scheme (PM POSHAN) and Anganwadi services, regular physical activity and regular health check-ups.
Body Systems, Common Diseases and the Sedentary Lifestyle

The body is made up of systems that work together: digestive, respiratory, circulatory, nervous, skeletal, muscular, excretory, endocrine, reproductive and immune systems. A problem in one system can affect others; for example, diabetes (endocrine) can damage the kidneys, eyes, nerves and heart.

Common communicable diseases include tuberculosis, malaria, dengue, hepatitis and diarrhoeal diseases. Common non-communicable diseases include hypertension, heart disease, stroke, diabetes, chronic respiratory disease and cancer. Non-communicable diseases are now the main cause of death in India.

A sedentary lifestyle, with long hours of sitting and screen time and little exercise, is a major risk factor for non-communicable diseases. It is linked to obesity, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, weak muscles and bones, back pain and depression.

Prevention includes at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week for adults, breaking up long periods of sitting, walking or cycling for short trips, playing sports, a healthy diet, avoiding tobacco and alcohol, and regular screening for blood pressure, blood sugar and weight.
Healthy Foods for the Prevention of Lifestyle Diseases

Lifestyle diseases such as cancer, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, obesity, diabetes and PCOS are strongly influenced by diet. A healthy plate should include vegetables and fruits, whole grains such as brown rice, millets and whole wheat, protein sources such as pulses, beans, fish, eggs and lean meat, and small amounts of healthy fats.

For hypertension and heart disease, reduce salt, pickles, processed snacks and fried foods, and eat more fruits, vegetables, whole grains and pulses. For diabetes and PCOS, choose low glycaemic index foods, avoid sugary drinks and sweets, eat regular balanced meals and control portion sizes. For obesity, reduce calorie-dense foods and increase fibre and physical activity.

For cancer prevention, the WHO's International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies processed meat as carcinogenic. Diets high in smoked, salted and processed foods, together with tobacco and alcohol, increase cancer risk. Mizoram has recorded some of the highest cancer incidence rates in India in national cancer registry reports, and tobacco use (including tuibur, tobacco-infused water), smoked meat and high-salt foods are commonly cited as risk factors.
In conclusion, simple daily choices, such as eating more vegetables, less salt and sugar, and fewer processed foods, can greatly reduce the risk of lifestyle diseases.
Stress, Anxiety, Depression and Factors Affecting Mental Health

Stress is the response to demands that a person feels are challenging. Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome describes three stages: alarm, resistance and exhaustion. Lazarus and Folkman's transactional model explains that stress depends on primary appraisal (is this a threat?) and secondary appraisal (can I cope?), and that coping can be problem-focused (solving the problem) or emotion-focused (managing feelings).

Anxiety is excessive worry and fear, and depression is persistent low mood with loss of interest and energy. Both are common, especially among young people, and both are treatable. The National Mental Health Survey of India (2015-16) found that about one in ten adults had a mental disorder, yet most did not receive treatment.

Factors affecting mental health include biological factors (genes, illness, hormones), psychological factors (coping skills, self-esteem, trauma) and social factors (family, peers, academic pressure, unemployment, poverty, discrimination, substance use, social media and stigma).

Ways to protect mental health include talking to trusted people, regular exercise, enough sleep, healthy eating, time management, relaxation and meditation, limiting alcohol and avoiding drugs, and seeking professional help when needed. The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, protects the rights of people with mental illness, and Tele-MANAS (14416) offers free counselling.
UNIT II — MANAGEMENT OF HEALTH AND WELLNESS
Physical fitness is the ability to carry out daily tasks with energy and alertness, without undue fatigue, and with enough reserve to enjoy leisure and meet emergencies.
In India, the Fit India Movement was launched on 29 August 2019 (National Sports Day) to encourage people to include physical activity in daily life.

Health-related fitness has five components: cardiorespiratory endurance (the heart and lungs supplying oxygen during sustained activity), muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition (the proportion of fat to lean mass).
Skill-related fitness includes agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time and speed. These are important for sports and also help prevent falls and injuries in daily life.

Regular exercise strengthens the heart and lungs, lowers blood pressure and cholesterol, helps control weight and blood sugar, strengthens bones and muscles, improves flexibility and posture, and boosts immunity.
It also improves mood, reduces stress, anxiety and depression, improves sleep and concentration, and builds self-confidence and social connections through sports and group activities.

Hypokinetic diseases are diseases associated with lack of physical activity ('hypo' means under and 'kinetic' means movement). The term was used by Hans Kraus and Wilhelm Raab in their book 'Hypokinetic Disease' (1961).

Examples include obesity, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, coronary heart disease, osteoporosis, lower back pain and depression. They have become more common with modern lifestyles involving desk work, motorized transport and long screen time.

Exercise programmes can follow the FITT principle: Frequency (how often), Intensity (how hard), Time (how long) and Type (what kind of exercise). A balanced programme includes aerobic exercise (walking, jogging, cycling, swimming, dancing), strength training (body-weight exercises, weights) at least twice a week, and flexibility and balance exercises (stretching, yoga).
People with existing conditions such as heart disease or diabetes should start slowly and take medical advice. Warming up before and cooling down after exercise reduce the risk of injury.
Posture is the position in which we hold our body while standing, sitting or lying down. Poor posture over a long time can lead to postural deformities.

Common postural deformities include kyphosis (an excessive outward curve of the upper back, or 'hunchback'), lordosis (an excessive inward curve of the lower back), scoliosis (a sideways curve of the spine), flat foot (absence of the arch of the foot), knock knees (genu valgum, knees touching while ankles are apart), bow legs (genu varum, knees apart while ankles touch) and forward head posture, sometimes called 'text neck', caused by looking down at phones.

General measures include sitting and standing straight, using a chair and desk of the right height, keeping screens at eye level, carrying school bags on both shoulders, regular exercise and avoiding long periods in one position.

Common corrective exercises include chest-opening stretches, back extensions and asanas such as bhujangasana and dhanurasana for kyphosis; abdominal strengthening, pelvic tilts and forward bends for lordosis; stretching and swimming for mild scoliosis; walking on toes, toe curls and rolling a ball under the foot for flat foot; and asanas such as padmasana and gomukhasana for knock knees. Severe deformities need medical treatment.

Spirituality refers to a sense of meaning and purpose in life, connection with something greater than oneself, and living by deeper values. It may be expressed through religion, prayer, worship, service, nature or reflection.

Spirituality can support mental health by giving hope, comfort in difficult times, a sense of belonging to a community and a moral framework. In Mizoram, church fellowship, prayer groups and the value of tlawmngaihna (helping others) provide such support. However, spiritual support should complement, not replace, professional help when someone has a mental illness.

Meditation is a practice of training attention and awareness to achieve a calm, clear and stable state of mind. Types include concentration meditation (focusing on the breath, a word or an object), mindfulness meditation (observing thoughts and feelings without judgement), loving-kindness meditation, yoga nidra and pranayama (breath control).

Research shows that regular meditation can reduce stress, anxiety and blood pressure, and can improve attention, emotional balance and sleep. Jon Kabat-Zinn's Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) programme, started in 1979, is widely used. The International Day of Yoga is observed on 21 June.

Sleep is essential for physical repair, growth, immunity, memory, learning and emotional balance. Sleep occurs in cycles of about 90 minutes, moving between non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, when most dreaming occurs.

Adults generally need 7-9 hours of sleep and teenagers 8-10 hours. Lack of sleep is linked to poor concentration, irritability, weak immunity, weight gain, accidents, depression and anxiety. Good sleep hygiene includes a regular sleep schedule, avoiding screens and caffeine before bed, a dark and quiet room, and regular physical activity. Insomnia can be treated with cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I).

Common mental illnesses include depression, anxiety disorders (generalized anxiety, panic disorder, phobias), obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), bipolar disorder (alternating episodes of depression and mania), schizophrenia (a severe disorder affecting thinking and perception), eating disorders and substance use disorders.

Warning signs include long-lasting sadness or irritability, withdrawal from friends and activities, sudden changes in sleep or appetite, a fall in academic performance, excessive worry, hearing or seeing things others do not, talk of self-harm and the use of alcohol or drugs to cope. Early identification and treatment improve recovery.

Substance abuse is the harmful use of psychoactive substances such as tobacco, alcohol and drugs (for example cannabis, heroin and methamphetamine). Repeated use can lead to dependence (addiction), where a person feels a strong craving and continues use despite harm.

Tobacco causes cancers, heart and lung diseases; alcohol damages the liver, heart and brain and is linked to accidents and violence; and drugs can cause overdose, infections such as HIV and hepatitis through shared needles, and mental illness. According to the Global Adult Tobacco Survey-2 (2016-17), Mizoram had the highest prevalence of tobacco use among adults of any Indian state. In India, tobacco is regulated by COTPA, 2003, and narcotic drugs by the NDPS Act, 1985.

De-addiction involves helping a person stop using a substance safely, sometimes with medical detoxification to manage withdrawal symptoms. Counselling helps the person understand the causes of their addiction, build motivation, learn coping skills and prevent relapse.

Rehabilitation helps the person return to normal life through continued therapy, family support, vocational training, self-help groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous and Narcotics Anonymous, and community support. The Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan (2020) and the National Tobacco Quitline (1800-11-2356) are national initiatives. In Mizoram, government de-addiction centres, churches, NGOs and the YMA run awareness and rehabilitation programmes.
Physical Fitness: Types and Health Benefits

Physical fitness is the ability to perform daily activities with energy and without undue fatigue. It has health-related components (cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition) and skill-related components (agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time and speed).

Different types of exercise build different components: aerobic exercise such as brisk walking, running, cycling, swimming and dancing builds endurance; strength training builds strength and endurance; stretching and yoga build flexibility; and sports and balance exercises build skill-related fitness.

The health benefits include a stronger heart and lungs, lower blood pressure and cholesterol, weight control, better blood sugar control, stronger bones, better posture, improved immunity, better sleep, reduced stress and depression, and improved concentration and self-esteem.

In conclusion, students should aim for regular, enjoyable activity, at least 60 minutes a day for those aged 5-17 and 150-300 minutes of moderate activity a week for adults, as part of a healthy lifestyle.

Modern life involves desk jobs, motorized transport, long screen time and easy access to processed foods. This has led to a rise in hypokinetic diseases, which are diseases associated with lack of physical activity, such as obesity, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, coronary heart disease, osteoporosis, back pain and depression.

Obesity results from more energy intake than expenditure. Type 2 diabetes is linked to obesity and inactivity, which reduce the body's sensitivity to insulin. Hypertension and heart disease are linked to inactivity, a poor diet, stress, tobacco and obesity. Osteoporosis, the weakening of bones, is worsened by a lack of weight-bearing exercise.

Prevention and management through exercise follow the FITT principle (Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type). Brisk walking, cycling, swimming, sports, strength exercises and yoga help prevent and manage these diseases. Small changes, such as using stairs, walking short distances and taking breaks from sitting, also help.
In conclusion, regular physical activity, combined with a healthy diet and avoidance of tobacco and alcohol, is the most effective and cheapest way to prevent hypokinetic diseases.

Good posture keeps the body balanced and reduces strain on muscles and joints. Poor posture, caused by bad sitting habits, heavy bags, lack of exercise, obesity, improper footwear, long phone use or, in some cases, birth defects and disease, can lead to postural deformities.

The main deformities are kyphosis (rounded upper back), lordosis (excessive inward curve of the lower back), scoliosis (sideways curve of the spine), flat foot, knock knees, bow legs and forward head posture ('text neck').

Corrective measures include correct sitting and standing habits, ergonomic furniture, keeping screens at eye level, carrying bags on both shoulders, and specific exercises: chest stretches and back extensions (bhujangasana, dhanurasana) for kyphosis; abdominal strengthening and pelvic tilts for lordosis; stretching and swimming for mild scoliosis; toe walking and toe curls for flat foot; and padmasana and gomukhasana for knock knees.
In conclusion, early correction is easier than later treatment, and severe or painful deformities should be examined by a doctor or physiotherapist.
Spirituality, Meditation and Sleep for Mental Health

Spirituality gives meaning, purpose, hope and a sense of belonging, which help people cope with stress and difficulties. Religious or spiritual communities, such as church fellowships in Mizoram, often provide social support during illness, bereavement and crisis.

Meditation trains attention and awareness. Mindfulness, concentration meditation, pranayama and yoga nidra can reduce stress, anxiety and blood pressure and improve focus and emotional balance. Even 10-15 minutes a day can be helpful.

Sleep is essential for physical and mental health. Adults need 7-9 hours and teenagers 8-10 hours. Poor sleep is linked to irritability, poor memory, weak immunity, weight gain, accidents, anxiety and depression. Good sleep hygiene includes regular sleep times, avoiding screens and caffeine before bed, and a comfortable sleep environment.
In conclusion, spirituality, meditation and sleep are simple, low-cost practices that support mental health, but they should be combined with professional help when a person has a mental illness.

Mental illnesses are health conditions involving changes in emotion, thinking or behaviour that cause distress or problems in functioning. They are classified in systems such as the WHO's ICD-11 and the American Psychiatric Association's DSM-5.

Common mental illnesses include depression, anxiety disorders, OCD, PTSD, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, eating disorders and substance use disorders. Warning signs include persistent sadness, withdrawal, changes in sleep and appetite, a decline in study or work, excessive fear or worry, unusual beliefs or perceptions, and talk of self-harm.

Stigma often prevents people from seeking help. The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, guarantees the right to mental health care and decriminalized attempted suicide. The District Mental Health Programme and Tele-MANAS (14416) provide services.
In conclusion, students should learn to recognize warning signs in themselves and others, respond with empathy, and encourage early professional help.
Substance Abuse, De-addiction, Counselling and Rehabilitation

Substance abuse is the harmful use of tobacco, alcohol and drugs. Causes include peer pressure, curiosity, stress, family problems, easy availability, mental health problems and the media. In Mizoram, the closeness to international drug trafficking routes has made drugs such as heroin and methamphetamine available, and tobacco use is very high.

Effects include physical disease (cancer, liver disease, lung and heart disease, HIV and hepatitis from shared needles), mental illness, accidents, crime, family breakdown, financial loss and death from overdose.

Treatment involves de-addiction (stopping use safely, sometimes with medical detoxification), counselling (individual, group and family therapy to build motivation and coping skills), and rehabilitation (vocational training, self-help groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous and Narcotics Anonymous, and reintegration into society). Relapse is common, so long-term support is important.

Prevention includes awareness programmes, life skills education, strong family and community support, sports and youth activities, and enforcement of laws such as COTPA (2003) and the NDPS Act (1985). The Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan (2020), the National Tobacco Quitline (1800-11-2356), and the work of the YMA, churches and NGOs in Mizoram support prevention and recovery.

For a short answer, define the term, give three to five points (types, causes, effects or measures) and add one example. For a long answer, use the order Meaning → Types or Causes → Effects → Prevention or Management → Conclusion. Where relevant, mention Indian programmes (POSHAN Abhiyaan, Fit India Movement, Tele-MANAS, Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan) and local examples from Mizoram, such as high tobacco use and the role of churches and the YMA.
